utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody. Like the last days, we are sitting only with two judges, pursuant to Rule 15 bis. I suppose the next witness is ready. He should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Boering. Welcome to the Tribunal, to the courtroom. I hope you will receive Dutch interpretation. Very good. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: {Witness answered through Interpreter]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Mr. Thayer has questions for you. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you and Your Honours; good afternoon to the Defence; good afternoon, everyone, and particularly to our Dutch interpreters. Always nice to have them with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Would you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Piet Boering.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And sir, do you recall testifying in this courtroom over a period of six days in September of 2006?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you recently read that testimony, which was in the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes. I reviewed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you attest that the transcripts that you reviewed accurately reflect what you said during your testimony in the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can remember, it describes accurately what took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you attest before this Trial Chamber that were you asked the same questions today that you were asked back in September of 2006, that your answers would be the same?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Well, basically, yes, but as things go further into the past, they become harder to remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And with that small qualification, can you attest that, to the best of your ability and to your knowledge and your recollection, if you were asked the same questions today that you were asked back in 2006, that your answers would be the same?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, I assume that to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender 65 ter numbers 6686 and 6687, the witness's prior testimony in the Popovic case, 6686 being under seal. And if I may make one correction to the dates that were listed on the Prosecution's exhibit list. The dates of his testimony were the 19th, 21st, 22nd, 25th, 26th, and 27th of September, 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. These two documents will be received into evidence, the first one under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. 65 ter 06686 shall be given Exhibit P01460 under seal, while 65 ter 06687 shall be given Exhibit P01461. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution does have a number of associated exhibits to tender with respect to this witness. I trust that the Trial Chamber and court officers have a copy of the Prosecution's exhibit list, which was distributed sometime ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, this is the list we received with all the exhibits you're tendering. These -- the documents will be received starting from 65 ter 06073, because the first one is already an exhibit, going through to the last one, 03331. These are the exhibits associated with the transcript in Popovic. They will be received and the Registry will provide you with the P numbers by e-mail in due course. I have to correct myself. Not by e-mail but by an internal memo.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And Mr. President, if I may address the final category of exhibits on the exhibit list, beginning with 6656, we will not be tendering that statement of another witness. That's already been -- the small portion from that statement was already read into the record. I think it's unnecessary to admit that or tender that. The video still of the sign taken from the building in Srebrenica is already part of the record through the Fontana video; and the UNMO report dated 9 July, again, the relevant portion was read fully into the record; and with respect to that final map 5, that is identical to map 5 in the map book in this case, which is Exhibit P104, So it's essentially the same as another document which has already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this information. And the video still, 65 ter 00426, is already an exhibit, P1136.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. President, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I have a 92 ter summary for the witness. The witness arrived in Srebrenica on 3 January 1995 as part of DutchBat. He held the rank of major and served as a liaison officer with the ABiH and VRS, the civilian leadership on both sides, and NGOs such as MSF, ICRC and UNHCR. VRS officers he met included Drina Corps commander General Zivanovic, Bratunac Brigade Major Momir Nikolic, with whom he met every two weeks, and Skelani Brigade commander Colonel Vukovic. The witness also met Colonel Beara twice, once between March and April, and once between May and June. Beara was interested in Naser Oric's whereabouts and role, and the structure of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, sorry for interrupting you. Perhaps it's better you use the other microphone because everybody will hear the sound of the typing on that table and this is perhaps a problem, especially for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart is continuing her memoirs. ABiH officers he met included Commander Naser Oric, Chief of Staff Ramiz Becirovic, Ekrem, a security officer who was sometimes in charge in Oric and Becirovic's absence, and Zulfo Tursunovic, who was the independent leader in the Bandera Triangle. The witness met with the ABiH leaders about once a week, but Becirovic quickly took over for Oric, whom the witness did not see after early or mid-February. Topics discussed included disarming people seen with weapons, smuggling, and maintenance of the weapons in the weapon collection point. The witness also described DutchBat's efforts to disarm people with weapons inside the enclave, smuggling of weapons and helicopter flights into the enclave, and complaints from the VRS about ABiH raids launched from inside the enclave outside the enclave. The witness described the humanitarian situation in the enclave and the deteriorating security situation in the months prior to the VRS attack in July 1995. In June, there were more shootings from the Serbian side into the enclave, and he received reports of people being injured and killed from the leadership of the local population and the hospitals. The situation deteriorated and people became more insecure and drew closer to each other within the city of Srebrenica. The witness also described the effects of VRS convoy restrictions on DutchBat. In addition, starting in late May and early June, DutchBat peacekeepers also faced direct fire at their vehicles, targeting just in front of or behind them, when leaving the compound. The witness described the events during the VRS attack on the enclave, including the movement of the civilian population into Srebrenica, the shelling of the Bravo Company compound in Srebrenica, the movement of the population from Srebrenica to the DutchBat compound in Potocari, the three Hotel Fontana meetings, the boarding of buses at Potocari on 12 July, being forced at gunpoint out of the "White House," separations of men near the Potocari compound as well as at the buses there, accompanying the first convoy to Kladanj and witnessing men being separated off of one of the buses near Tisca in the direction of the woods by Milici Brigade soldiers in the presence of Major Sarkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I have some follow-up questions concerning some things you've said in your prior testimony and statements. First, can you just tell the Trial Chamber, are you still in active service in the military; and if so, what's your rank and your current position or function?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Well, I'm still in the Dutch military. At this point, I'm -- at this point I have a different rank. I'm not a colonel yet. I'm presently working in Enschede at the centre of excellence in the cooperation between military and civilians in -- within NATO, in the EU, and I've just returned from a seven-month mission in Kabul, at the headquarters. My rank is lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to go through a number of small quick topics, just to add some detail to some issues that the Trial Chamber has heard a little bit about already. In 1995, during your tour in Srebrenica, can you describe, just briefly, the division of labour between you and Sergeant Major Rave.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Generally, we would go off together and would prepare the discussions and meetings about the situation, and we would also compile the reports together. You might say that my role was more that of civil -- maintaining civilian contacts and being the liaison officer as well, and Sergeant Rave's tasks highlighted intelligence more. But both areas were necessary to maintain an overall impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So, in fact, were both of you essentially serving in a liaison capacity? Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes. You could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, in the Popovic trial - and this is at transcript page 1869 - you described a speech which General Zivanovic gave early upon your arrival in the enclave in early 1995. Can you tell the Trial Chamber in as much detail as you can, what General Zivanovic said. In the Popovic trial you didn't go into very much detail, and if you could provide a little bit more detail, as best you can remember, about what it was that he said, that would be helpful, I think, for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I can still remember those meetings that General Zivanovic attended. I remember that he made it clear that, in his view, the Srebrenica enclave should be returned to the Serbs, especially because he had lived there and he felt that he had a right to live safely there again and, in his view, that was not possible at this time. And he believed that we were -- we figured in that situation as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall what, if anything, he told you would happen if the enclave were not demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: What I remember is that he insisted that we had a role in that process, and if we couldn't fulfil that, then conceivably they would have to do it themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me see if I can jog your memory about a couple more details about what he said. If we could have 65 ter 6690, please. Sir, what we have up on the screen is your signed witness statement from February of 1998. Do you remember meeting with OTP investigators in February of 1998 and providing a statement?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could go to page 3 in both the original and B/C/S, we see in the first full paragraph in English, it's a paragraph that begins, "General Zivanovic delivered a long speech during the reception ..." Do you see that paragraph, sir?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes. I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And the second sentence reads: "He also said that the enclave had to be demilitarised by DutchBat, otherwise it would be razed to the ground." Do you recall General Zivanovic saying that during the speech, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I remember that he became very emotional and very angry and that he was aggressive in his statements, and the terms as it reads here convey that well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, these words "razed to the ground," are those your words or are those General Zivanovic's words?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: If I remember clearly, those were his words. Certainly not my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move to another topic. Sir, do you recall the Yellow Bridge check-point that was manned by the VRS nearby the DutchBat OP-Papa?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether there was one VRS soldier in particular who manned that check-point; and if so, what his name was?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes. I spent a lot of time with that individual that was the local commandant, Jovo, a former secondary school teacher, if I remember correctly. He was somewhat older.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Next topic: You testified about one of the UN interpreters who was employed in July of 1995, a young man who was Serbian by the name of Petar. Do you recall him and testifying about him in the last trial, sir?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I remember him all too well. I remember that he spent time in Bratunac, especially in Bratunac. Specifically what I stated about him doesn't come to mind at this time. He was present at most of the meetings, and he regularly exchanged messages with me, so he was a relatively important contact for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you remember learning or hearing that Petar was related to anyone in particular?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Well, yes. He was a relative, I believe but I'm not positive at this time, I believe he was related to Major Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you refer to Major Nikolic, you're referring to Momir Nikolic of the Bratunac Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes. I mean Momir Nikolic of the Bratunac Brigade, and we had regular contact to a lesser extent with him too. But he was the direct contact for the VRS, the Republika Srpska, among the officers. He was our regular contact among the officers, our point of contact there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Next topic, sir: When you first met Colonel Beara, and you testified in Popovic about your contacts, who introduced you to Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, Major Nikolic, Momir Nikolic, was present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did Momir Nikolic indicate to you what Colonel Beara's function or position was?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: No. With respect to both his own position and those of others, other members of the military, Momir Nikolic was very closed, and if you asked him, for example, what his own position was, he would become very disconcerted, agitated, angry. He didn't want that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And based on your contacts with Colonel Beara, did you form an impression or a conclusion, based on those contacts, about what Colonel Beara's function was in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Well, extensive conversations with Colonel Beara, once at Jovo and then again in Fontana, especially the second time, it became clear that Colonel Beara was focused on acquiring information about military operations, structures, the stay of Naser Oric, helicopter movements. The first time he came to OP-Papa, I remember he was more forthcoming about possible planning of operations and that these things had to happen and that, later on, we would be grateful to the VRS for that. He indicated that in very general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So based on those conversations and what he was telling you, did you have or did you draw any conclusions about what his -- what Colonel Beara's actual function or position was, what kind of an officer he was in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Well, you could clearly tell that he was higher in rank than the Bratunac Brigade, and even higher up in the staff than Zivanovic. When I spoke with him, Momir Nikolic would -- would keep to the background and would not cooperate with the conversation at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were you able to gain any impression of what or to which organ of the VRS Colonel Beara belonged?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Well, I conveyed that information to my own headquarters, with the names, and I don't remember providing any feedback about his role and function. But that he was affiliated with the higher levels, conceivably with the higher military institutions, that was very clear. He dealt with the institutions in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you recall that DutchBat had a contract with the Hotel Fontana to obtain food and beverages?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that, and according to that contract, we would try once a week to have a truck load full of soft drinks, cigarettes, and perhaps other food, we would try to buy that, because our own provisions were too limited. This was because the supply of all kinds of provisions was blocked by clearances that were not issued or were issued in very limited measure by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And before we turn to the events of July 1995, sir, just one additional question: You provided some more detail a moment ago about General Zivanovic's speech and what he said the VRS would do to Srebrenica if the enclave were not demilitarised. I want to read a question and answer that you gave during an interview with NIOD on September -- I beg your pardon, 17 December 2001. We don't need to put it on e-court, it's not on our exhibit list, I'm just going to read it to you. I've advised the Defence about this particular provision. You were asked, and this is at page 41, paragraphs 679 and 680, you were asked: "Were there also warnings sometimes during the contacts with the Bosnian Serbs? We talked about it a little last time but were there specific warnings?" And your answer was: "Warnings? In any case, there was very often the offer. You can leave the enclave with as many women and children as possible, and I believe men too, as long as they are not soldiers. There is no point in you staying here. It has to come to an end. Threats, such as We will get it back again, yes, the first message, this is ours, they have no business here, was at the beginning of January, with Zivanovic who was very emotional. I was born here and this is my place. They have no business here." Let me just stop right there. In this answer, sir, where you were referring to General Zivanovic, is this the same speech that you told us about a few moments ago?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: If you're referring to the fact that offers were regularly made for the population to leave the enclave freely, yes, that offer was made repeatedly by different individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Such as? If you can recall.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Well, I think it would have been Beara, Nikolic -- Momir Nikolic -- Zivanovic. It was a regularly recurring topic of conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And you go on in your answer and you say: "And then there was reasoning as to whether or not this is my territory. Later, like I already said on Friday, on one occasion during Easter, an unfamiliar colonel-type man from Pale said, and I quote, 'You'll be grateful to us. Be calm, we'll settle this, this is our territory after all.'" Can you tell us anything more about this colonel from Pale? Do you have any recollection about a name or function? If not, that's fine. I'll just move on.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: This is the individual mentioned earlier in this interrogation, Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And finally in your answer, you state: "Also, conversations during the visits to the hospital, the director of the hospital, who had a lot of drink on board, then you could notice that there was enormous hatred, racism or whatever you want to call it," and here you're quoting this individual, and I quote, "They have no right to exist, they have to be killed off." And then you continue your answer: "No remorse whatsoever if that happened." Now my first question to you, sir, is do you recall this conversation with this person from the hospital? And does the answer that I just read to you accurately reflect what this person said?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I remember that visit to that hospital, the tenor of his discourse, and I assume that he did, in fact, say something like that. Hate was clearly present, especially from what I remember in that hospital over there. Many deliberate abortions were performed. I remember the population couldn't adequately take care of babies, and he indicated that that was certainly not happening in the enclave, and he thought it was horrible that the population in the enclave was growing, and that the activities were increasing --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me: The threats were increasing.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you refer to the population not being able to take care of babies, are you referring to the Serb population or the Muslim population inside the enclave?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I'm referring to the hospital where abortions were taking place, that was outside the enclave in Bratunac. I'm referring to the Serb population. So outside the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just to be specific, the director to whom you were speaking, which hospital was he the director of?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: He was the director of the hospital in Bratunac. We were visiting there to find out whether we could provide some kind of support in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, the words in your answer, and I quote again, "They have no right to exist. They have to be killed off," are those your words or are those his words, sir?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Those were his words.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's turn to the events in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, just for the sake of the record, could you please put the 65 ter exhibit number on the record, of the document you have read out to the witness many parts of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: For this document, Mr. President, this is not on the 65 ter list. I advised the Defence beforehand that I would be reading this one paragraph from it, but it's been disclosed for some time but not on the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn your attention to the 11th of July, when the civilian population was moving from the town of Srebrenica up to Potocari. You testified in the Krstic trial - and this is at transcript page 1161, for the Defence - that the population, in your words or word, was "expelled" from Srebrenica to Potocari. What did you mean by saying that they were expelled from Srebrenica to Potocari, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: What I mean by that is that the city of Srebrenica was jam-packed with people, Muslims. From what I could see, they had been driven out of the areas around Srebrenica into the city, in the hope of being able to stay there safely. And in the city, around the 10th, the situation also was perceived as too threatening, and grenades were dropped here and there, there was shooting, and reports of attacks by Serbs on the city of Srebrenica circulated among the population. Also, the impression of the DutchBat units was that purges were taking place, so the population in the city felt too unsafe and hoped for protection in the -- at the actual DutchBat camp in Potocari because, in the city of Srebrenica, there was a small company of DutchBat but nearby at least one grenade attack took place, so it wasn't safe there either and it was, in any case, too small.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, when you use the word "grenade," what are you talking about; a hand grenade or some other type of explosive?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I mean a different type of explosive; mortar grenades.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's turn for a few moments to the Hotel Fontana meetings which you attended and testified about at some length in the last trial. Before you entered the first meeting, you testified that you managed to make your way into the room where a number of DutchBat peacekeepers were being held hostage. Can you describe the appearance of those peacekeepers for the Trial Chamber, sir. What was their situation? How did they look to you? Could you provide a little bit more detail than you did in the Popovic trial?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I remember that in a room there was a group of about ten DutchBat servicemen who were -- they did not have any freedom of movement. They were in a room, and at the exit was an armed Serb, and he had to be there. They were seated at tables and were supposed to be served a meal. They indicated that they were the people from the observation posts who had been taken by the Serbs and subsequently involuntarily transported to Bratunac. So these were soldiers who were not free to move: Their vehicle had been taken from them, their materials had been taken from them, and they felt threatened. And of course, before they had been taken a prisoner of war by the Serbs, so to speak, they had also been confronted with targeted attacks by the Serbs, who had shot at them, and they were overpowered by the adversary. So they were certainly in a well -- in a state, they felt threatened, desperate. They hoped that they would be allowed to leave with us but they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. In your Popovic testimony, you testified about when you first arrived at the meeting, that there were some VRS officers and Mladic driving Colonel Karremans into a corner and that you tried to create some space. Can you again just provide the Trial Chamber with a little bit more detail about what you did in these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Karremans was there with Sergeant Major Rave in a corner. They were pressed into the corner, with a -- they were surrounded by a great many Serb military. There was a camera crew present, and it was made clear by Mladic that he was in charge and that he could do anything he wanted with us. So at that point he was clearly heaping threats upon threats.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And so physically, sir, what, if anything, did you do to create space, as you put it in the last trial?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Well, you try to create additional space and to push people aside a bit, and I tried to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you referred, in your Popovic testimony, to a VRS officer by the name of Kosovic or Kosoric. I think you used both names in your prior testimony. Can you describe him physically for the Trial Chamber, please. Was there anything notable that you recall about his physical appearance?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Well, he had a normal build, but bold, a big mustache, a tattoo of an anchor or a mortar on his arm, and he smoked a cigarette pipe shaped like a mortar shell, was engraved in that. He was clearly recognisable.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you refer to a "cigarette pipe," are you referring to a cigarette holder, sir, sort of the old-fashioned cigarette holder that you insert a cigarette into the end of?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What did you understand his role to be at that time and over the next day or so?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: He was, in fact, involved in planning and carrying out convoys to drive the Muslim population out of the enclave. He was the logistics person in charge of organising the buses, trucks, transport.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall from whom you received authorisation or permission on the ground to escort that first convoy that you testified about in Popovic?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: He was certainly present with the first convoy, Popovic, and so was Mladic, and a vehicle was to ride in the front and at the rear. Kosovic was present -- excuse me, it's not Popovic, it's Kosovic. I see that I misstated a name.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say that Mladic was present with the first convoy, do you mean he was present with the first convoy in Potocari or do you mean that Mladic accompanied the first convoy with you and Kosovic or Kosoric?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Kosovic accompanied the first convoy. Mladic was present at the departure.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was Colonel Kosoric or Kosovic's presence any kind of factor in the convoy's ability to cross through check-points as the convoy made its way from Potocari to Tisca?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I think that he was one of the organisers responsible for ensuring that the convoy would take place as quickly as possible. I remember that at a certain point we stopped because there was a conflict, there was shooting in the area, it was unsafe, and if I remember correctly, he was involved in resolving the matter as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see that I have just met my one hour estimate. I have just a couple more questions. With the Court's indulgence, if I could complete my examination. I just have a couple more questions and topics along this line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is really an improvement, Mr. Thayer. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, in your experience, sir, during your tour of duty with DutchBat, how easy was it to travel across VRS-held territory?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: It was virtually impossible for us to drive around freely. A route would be released through a clearance at certain times, and we were not allowed to deviate from that. Even if you had a clearance and a section of time, even then there could be disturbances to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in your experience, how often would you hit check-points? Was it a common occurrence or an uncommon occurrence?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I didn't drive around that much myself in the area where the VRS might have set up check-points, but along the route with the refugees, in Kladanj, we ultimately encountered a few check-points.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me: On the way to Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And on this trip, do you recall it being of any help, in terms of passing through those check-points, to have an officer such as this Colonel Kosovic or Kosoric with you?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Well, I think that he was the driving force.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Just a couple more questions, sir. You testified about a Colonel Jankovic, who was present at the Fontana meetings. Did anyone inform you what his role was at the time and was going to be over the next day or so?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, at the first meeting in Fontana, Mladic and Jankovic were present, and Mladic, at the start of the meeting, introduced Colonel Jankovic as his support, somebody who had studied law and was very capable of handling all matters in a legally appropriate manner, and over the course of the days that followed, perhaps Mladic wouldn't be present because he had other affairs to handle, and that from then on, the command would be entrusted to Colonel Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's just quickly look at some photographs. If we could have P624 -- and actually, let me withdraw that. Let's not show P624. Just for the record, Mr. President, I'm going to ask, as we've done in previous cases, the witness to look at two photographs that are in P624, which is the video stills book. The Trial Chamber will remember that that has the identities listed, so we are now going to show the witness through Sanction the underlying photographs without the identifications and I'm just going to ask Colonel Boering to make some identifications. And we are first talking about page 27, just for the record, of that P624, and Ms. Stewart will show us an image. And it has the ERN 0291-6181. Sir, do you recognise anyone in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I recognise both General Mladic and Colonel Jankovic to the right, or, rather, to his left.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just to be clear, Jankovic is sitting to the left of General Mladic. Is that what you just told us?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we may have the next photograph, and this is page 37 of P624, can you identify anyone in this photograph that you recall, sir? And let's start from the left, moving towards the right of the image.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I'm the one wearing the T-shirt there. Next to me is the spokesman for the women, Camila, and next to her, a representative of the men, Nuhanovic, and at the head of the table, with the mustache, is the man we mentioned earlier, Kosovic, who was chiefly involved in logistics. And then you see some heads, mainly of the civilians working for the police and the municipal authorities of Bratunac, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. For the record, this is ERN 0291-6189. Thank you, we are done with that exhibit. Now, you testified in Popovic that Mladic mentioned screenings or separations of men, certainly you said during the third Fontana meeting, if not earlier. Did General Mladic mention any particular age range?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: He mentioned the age group of men from age 16 to age 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And for my last question, Colonel, you spoke about, in your witness statement that we had on the screen earlier, and this is at page 11 of the English and 10 of the B/C/S, just for the record, do you remember an encounter between General Mladic and the director of MSF? And we don't need to put her name on the record, but do you remember an encounter between General Mladic and that person in Potocari on the 12th of July? And if so, can you just describe for the Trial Chamber the circumstances of that encounter.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, I remember her. I also remember what her envisaged role was and that she did not get that leeway at all from General Mladic. I'll start by describing her role. At the time, the transport, the buses and trucks had arrived to evacuate the Muslim population, and the idea was that first the injured and the sick would be evacuated, and she was a strong advocate of that, in part at the request of Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans, and that message she tried to convey to General Mladic was not accepted at all. She was told to mind her own business and to watch out. She was basically threatened because things would be taken care of anyway and her involvement wasn't requested and was certainly not necessary and was definitely not appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall stating in your witness statement, and I quote: "He said that she better keep out of it, otherwise he could do anything to her he wanted"? Do you remember General Mladic saying that to her?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I was there, and he did, in fact, threaten her. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, now Mr. Tolimir is commencing his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to greet all those present. I would like for peace to reign in this house, and I hope these proceedings today end not as I will but as God wills.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to welcome the witness and thank him for testifying today. Sir, we are going to start with the last question that Mr. Thayer put to you today. He asked you on page 22, line 18, were you present when General Mladic said that he could do anything to her? In your last answer, on page 22, line 15, you said, "I remember he threatened her." Can you please tell us, did he state the words that Mr. Thayer used in his question, or do you just recollect that in some way he threatened her? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: At this time, I certainly don't remember the exact words, but they were definitely words with this clear intent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 20, line 2, Mr. Thayer asked you whether there was any help during crossing of the check-points. You had an officer with you like General Kosoric or Kosovic, I'm not sure which surname he used. My question is: This colonel who was with you, by the name of Kosoric or Kosovic, who was with you, I'm not sure, was it his task also to take the column safely through the territory of Republika Srpska? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: What the -- what would be done and where we were going was not made clear to us at the start; who was responsible and who arranged everything, that was the VRS under the aegis of Kosovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he organise that or was this agreed at the meeting in Fontana? Are you able to tell this to the Trial Chamber? Arranged between the representatives of the army and the representatives of the Muslim civilian population that were going from Republika Srpska through the Republic of Croatia to the Federation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: At the meeting in Fontana, it was agreed that the population could leave the enclave safely and that this would happen under escort by DutchBat. The exact details were not elaborated at that meeting, at least not as far as I remember. When we returned from the meeting in Fontana, I asked Lieutenant Colonel Karremans about the specifics of the transport agreements. This was not clear to him either. And subsequently, after consulting Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans, I returned to Fontana to sort out the details or obtain them so that we could focus our approach. Upon my arrival in Fontana, I encountered Momir Nikolic and he said to me, "What are you doing here? You have no business here. Everything has been settled sometime ago. Don't worry." And by then, the buses and trucks were already crossing Bratunac toward Potocari. So to get back to your question as to exactly what was agreed at the meeting in Fontana, yes, agreements were reached there but not very clear ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you present at that meeting in Fontana, you and Colonel Kosoric who left with the first group of the population that was evacuating Srebrenica and going to Kladanj? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the discussions between the civilian representatives and the army, was the name of Kladanj mentioned at all? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I was present at those conversations. The interpreter, Petar, was seated a bit away from me, so I wasn't fully able to follow some of the discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And was Mr. Nikolic present at the meeting, whom you refer -- to whom you refer in your statement? This is 65 ter 0673. Can we show the witness that statement, please. You talk about that on page 7, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just to clarify, that's 6703.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We can see that statement. Can we see page 7 now in the Serbian, and Aleksandar will say the page number in English. Thank you. We can see paragraph 3. I can see it, where you talk about how you returned with Nikolic, and then at the end you say, "He was not able to tell us how many buses would be available." Perhaps you can look at that part in the English and the interpreter then will translate it back to you. Can we show page 7 in the English, please, paragraph 3. And we can see that now. This is that paragraph, the last paragraph where they talk about 1400 hours. Aleksandar, please, can you please tell us what page that is? Thank you. So the question is did Nikolic tell you - I'm quoting - in the last sentence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In English, it's the top of page 8 I think is where General Tolimir wants to be. It's the top of page 8, referring to the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the last sentence, the -- Nikolic told you, I quote, "He could not tell me how many buses would be available." Based on what you wrote in your statement, could we conclude that Nikolic didn't know this either, just like you didn't, and Kosoric?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: No. I would not assume that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you say what I quoted back to you, "He was not -- he could not tell me how many buses would be available"? This is something that I read from page 7, paragraph 3. Thank you. And can I ask the interpreter to read to you in Dutch the last sentence on page 7, paragraph 3. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was translated, interpreted to the witness in Dutch. Whatever you are reading will be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, you said that. I didn't say it. I mean, your answer now, when you said that you would not assume that, is that now a contradiction in terms of what you said earlier in your statement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I would say that it's not a contradiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... say that Nikolic did not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to clarify this. It seems to be a confusion at the moment. We see in this paragraph of your statement to the OTP of 1995, and I quote, "He could not tell me how many buses would be available." And Mr. Tolimir wants to know if that is true that this man Mr. Nikolic couldn't tell you how many buses would be available or if you know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I arrived there and sought Nikolic, no interpreter was present and it was very difficult to talk with Nikolic. In any case, he indicated that aside from how the statement reads there, from what I remember, the number of buses -- that he didn't know that, but that there would be buses and there would be transport and, "Get lost because it's going to happen anyway now."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you ask him about the number of buses available for the transportation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked him, of course, for details about buses and transport and other things, but he did not see any reason to answer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I think that this is not really of such importance, so we will move on to something else. But I believe, and maybe you can help us, that no one really knew at the time how many buses would arrive, and would it have been the case, in fact, that depending on the number of buses that did arrive, that number of civilians actually were put on the buses and sent away? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: There was talk of several convoys until the population had been evacuated, and how long it would take, that depended on fuel and vehicles, and I remember that General Mladic had urged DutchBat to supply fuel because the operation would require a lot of fuel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we are running out of time. We are over time already. We must have our first break now. I just wanted to give you the opportunity to finish with this topic, but it's now necessary to break. But I would like to raise for a moment another question. I was told that we could sit tomorrow in the morning instead of in the afternoon, because the courtroom is available, another trial has cancelled the sitting of tomorrow. Perhaps you can consider this question during the break. There would be one real advantage, we don't know if we are coming under time pressure at the end of this witness and his testimony again, and the availability of the interpreters is of high importance, and perhaps we can then be sure to finish this witness tomorrow, if we are sitting in the morning instead of in the afternoon. We come back to that later. Please consider that during the break. We break now and resume 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we first deal with the question of sitting tomorrow in the morning or in the afternoon. What is the position of the parties? Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We will be ready tomorrow morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as far as we are concerned, it is all right. The only issue is that if a document has not already been entered in e-court, if we can be allowed to look them over overnight because they have already been used in the Popovic case. And the only reason -- my only problem is the e-court because I have to take a look at all the documents that will need to be entered in e-court or those that have already been entered into e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At the moment I'm not quite sure what your concern is but I think Mr. Gajic will assist you, providing you with all necessary documents, in e-court or in hard copy, as it was in the past already. I think we --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. But I have to read those documents in order to be able to formulate my questions because I have to read them over again and see if I can identify them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understand you very well, and that was the reason why I raised this problem, because we are sitting in the afternoon today and that would be a hearing tomorrow morning. The problem is -- are you objecting the move of the hearing to the morning or not? If you are objecting, we have to consider your position.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I am not objecting at all. I would like to help and be of assistance to the interpreters, who should be available here, and I will try to cooperate as much as I can. The only problem that I might have is to do with the documents and the e-court. That's all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The advantage of sitting in the morning, as I already mentioned, that the interpreters will be here and we don't come again in this situation that we have to adjourn and call the witness again next year, with the interpreters. If we are sitting in the afternoon, there is a clear time limit. If we are sitting in the morning, there would be a possibility for an extended sitting to finish the examination of this witness. Therefore, the Chamber is inclined to sit in the morning instead of in the afternoon. I take it that you are not objecting and therefore the Chamber decides to sit in the morning and the preparations necessary for that can be arranged. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Of course. Sorry, I didn't discuss it with you, sir. Are you available tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that sounds like a reasonable question to me. I understand that it's more convenient to settle this. I would have liked to have had a say in this, but I'll abide by your ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I apologise, not having asked you first. Of course it is a question of your availability. Would it be possible for you to appear tomorrow in the morning at 9.00 in the courtroom or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is, but to spend an entire day here, that means that after the break we might continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, this is not the idea of this decision. We want to finish with your examination in the morning session, until 1.45, but sometimes it happens that there are some additional questions, especially in re-examination by the Prosecution, that we can sit, for instance, half an hour longer, and that is only possible if we are sitting in the morning and not in the afternoon. That's all. We want to finish in time, at the end of the morning session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I understood. Agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When we left off, we were talking about whether the lieutenant-colonel or colonel who was with you was helpful when you crossed over the territory of Republika Srpska, and my new question is: Was his presence, the colonel's presence, Colonel Kosoric, was it of assistance to you and to the convoy or not?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: He was in command of the convoy, and I observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, was it logical for him to be in command of it while you were going through Republika Srpska? Because he was not in command while you were on the territory of the Federation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean by "the Federation."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, I am referring to when you continued with the convoy on and on the line of separation the colonel who had accompanied you until then actually went back and you went on on your own. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I don't understand the question, but of course the person in charge of the convoy is responsible for it. When we arrived to proceed to the line of separation, another individual was present, a liaison officer, I believe, of the Militia Brigade [as interpreted]. If I remember correctly, that was Major Sarkic, and I dealt with him there, no longer with Colonel Kosovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have, I think, a little problem with the transcript, which we have very frequently with this particular word that I believe the witness used, and it's at line 32 -- sorry, page 32, line 4, there is a reference to the Militia Brigade and I'm pretty confident that's not the word he used. It's a difficult one to hear, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Boering, you heard the comment on Mr. Thayer. Could you clarify to which structure you were referring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to the militia Brigade, that's a unit in the western -- that was present in the western part, in the area where the convoy was, and from there I walked with the refugees to Kladanj. The Milici Brigade, that's a unit in a certain area just as in Bratunac you have a Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, that was the problem. Now you were referring to the Milici Brigade. Was it always the Milici Brigade you were referring to or the Militia Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Milici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That clarifies the situation. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On page 17, line 17, Mr. Thayer asked you to tell him what you knew about Colonel Kosovic, and on page 18, line 7, you said, "He participated in planning, in the organisation of the convoy when the Muslim population left, and he was in charge of organising the transport and the logistics." My question, based on what you said, is: Are you sure of what you have said, that this colonel did, the colonel that Mr. Thayer asked you about? Are you sure that that's what he was in charge of and that he took part in organising the convoy and the evacuation of the civilian population from Potocari to Kladanj? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes. I'm certain of that, and I believe that he was even proposed for that by General Mladic. He was introduced for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When was he proposed for that task by General Mladic? Can you tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps this is again a translation issue. I realise that the witness corrected the word "proposed" into "introduced." Is that correct, Mr. Boering?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct. And that introduction, from what I remember, took place at the meeting in the morning at 10.00 a.m., where the population representatives were present and General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Boering. Can you tell us, please, whether during the meeting or before the meeting it was known what the decision by the representatives of the Muslims would be and what the decision would be that would issue or come as an issue out of this meeting that was held at Hotel Fontana?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: It was not my impression that the representatives of the Muslims felt that they had the power to decide anything. That's why, after the first round, when only one individual was present, he felt too insecure and needed support and found such support in two other persons in the population. In fact, the idea that they would be in a position to decide anything, that was not relevant. It was more an attempt to try to provide the population that was present with the best possible humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us now who provided humanitarian aid to the Muslim population? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: If we are talking about the situation of the local population, then the prospects were indeed very grim; insufficient food, insufficient medical supplies, and actual support was virtually non-existent because convoys with aid provisions were denied permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please answer my question. You said that the population received some humanitarian aid. Who was it who provided humanitarian aid to the population, in a situation where they were left without anything, in order for them to get something? Who was it who provided that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: The party providing aid was the UNHCR convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that you're referring to the situation before Potocari, but who was it who provided humanitarian aid that you referred to in the earlier -- in your earlier answer, when the population was in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I would like to refer you to the real answer that Mr. Boering gave, page 34, lines 12 to 14. He said, "It was more an attempt to try to provide the population that was present with the best possible humanitarian aid." He was talking about the attempt. Perhaps that is the difference. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for clarifying this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Boering, please tell us who made these attempts, who made the effort to try and provide humanitarian aid to these people and in the situation in which you found ourselves with such a great number of people in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Personally, I did not see any aid provisions entering after the enclave fell. Not from UNHCR, not from any other party. The population evacuated in the first convoy definitely did not have its primary needs provided for upon its departure. They were rushed into vehicles with a lot of pressure, time-wise, and then left without any humanitarian aid. At least, I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Boering. Are you actually referring to specific humanitarian aid in the physical sense or are you referring to the situation where you found yourself in view of some several thousand of people in Potocari who needed help? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: This question is not clear to me, but I'll try to answer it. This concerned the thousands of people who did not receive humanitarian aid at the time I was still there, and I'm referring to food, drinks, medical supplies, shelter, and whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The Trial Chamber will decide on what it was that you meant but my question to you is whether the UNPROFOR or the Muslims who participated in the negotiations could do anything to resolve the situation without the assistance of the VRS, the Army of Republika Srpska, in order to assist the population in that situation.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I think that if enough convoys with aid provisions could be brought in, the primary needs would certainly have been alleviated. And I'm referring, for example, to the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether there were any agreements on the movements of either humanitarian aid or UNPROFOR that had been signed by the VRS, the Army of Republika Srpska? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Well, I'm not aware of that. I was only in touch with the UNHCR staff member on site in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we quickly take a look at D77, that's a document that I drafted, and we will -- we have already entered it in the e-court. This is the agreement on the movement of these organisations. So I would just like to show it briefly to the witness. That's D77. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this document that deals with the principles for the freedom of movement?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I have seen some documents, and we regularly talked about convoys and related issues, but at this time I certainly can't remember whether I read this document. It's perfectly possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just take a look at (a), the first and second line: "UNPROFOR will notify the Serbian army authorities 48 hours in advance of convoy movements and 24 hours for single vehicles." Did you have such information?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Did you have such an obligation?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: There were procedures for requesting convoys. I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We can see that item 2 deals with movements, item 3 with control. Can we now see the last page? I want to put it to you that this was also signed by UNPROFOR. Thank you. Can you see that this movement was signed on the 31st of January, 1995? Well, first of all, were you in Srebrenica at the time? And we can see that it was signed by Brigadier General Brinkman and Major General Tolimir. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that all the provisions in this agreement were an obligation both for the UNPROFOR and for the Army of Republika Srpska, in view of the fact that the agreement was signed both by General Brinkman and by myself?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: This document indicates how to deal with convoys. I remember that in practice requesting -- the convoy requests from us and from UNPROFOR was otherwise, and permission was regularly rejected for convoys, so convoys were not allowed to proceed by the VRS. The VRS regularly withheld permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you give an example or can you give any reason to the Trial Chamber why the VRS would do that? Because it says here that if the Army of Republika Srpska denied passage to a convoy, they would need to state their reasons for doing that.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I think you'd need to ask the VRS, not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I would kindly ask you to answer this question: Without the permission of Army of Republika Srpska, was any convoy able to enter Srebrenica, regardless of whether it was an UNPROFOR convoy or a convoy of some humanitarian organisation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I think permission was required, and clearance was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And this permission or clearance by the Army of Republika Srpska for convoys to cross its territory, for them to escort it through, was that -- did that constitute any kind of assistance in getting the convoys and the aid to the population? Did that count as any kind of help? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: If a convoy could, in fact, proceed, then that certainly helped provide humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you able to say whether the passage of an oil pipeline is paid for through the countries of Russia, former Russia, the European Union, and so on? Do those countries have to pay for that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I don't understand this question, and I certainly haven't worked on that subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter kindly asks Mr. Tolimir to repeat his question. We were unable to quite follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We have the answer, Mr. President. I just want to note, from our perspective, if we have any hope of finishing tomorrow sometime, the fewer questions that are of that nature, dealing with issues like oil pipelines through other countries, the fewer of those, the better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we are dealing with this situation of the former Yugoslavia. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Are you aware that, during the war, gas was delivered to Bosnia and Herzegovina from Russia, and do you know if UNPROFOR participated in this endeavour? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: No. I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that Russia provided gas free of charge for Sarajevo and that Republika Srpska permitted the transport of that gas on Russia's proposal? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Mr. President, it's precisely what I stood up for, or about, a couple of minutes ago. Unless General Tolimir can clearly and, hopefully, quickly show what relevance this has to any issue in this case, I would ask that these types of questions stop. Otherwise, we are just going to be here forever on these types of unrelated topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Boering, do you recall the question? Have you any knowledge on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no knowledge of that. Especially in the Srebrenica enclave, this was not an issue, didn't play any role at all. Nor did I see any gas or oil pipelines that extended into the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, as you have the answer of the witness, you should move to another topic. He has no knowledge of this area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Thayer questioned the relevance. If UNPROFOR provides humanitarian aid to that population, why wouldn't the Army of Republika Srpska not do the same?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand you, Mr. President, but I'm talking about the relevance. If the UNHCR is providing assistance from their office, why wouldn't the Army of Republika Srpska do the same? But, Mr. President, I have been charged with not providing humanitarian aid while the Army of Republika Srpska was providing humanitarian aid, and even the witness said that the evacuation was a type of humanitarian aid and without the participation of the Army of Republika Srpska could not have been realised at all. And one side cannot provide assistance and then the other side can. They either both did. If UNPROFOR provided assistance, then so did Republika Srpska, the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I repeat: You have got the answer of this witness, he doesn't have any knowledge about that, and you should move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, since you said that the evacuation of the population was a form of humanitarian assistance, which was left without food and water and there were a large number of these people in a small place, would not humanitarian aid be considered to be offered by the party from whose territory the population, with that party's assistance, was transferred to a different territory? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: That's a possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please, a short moment. We have to discuss a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry for that. Mr. Boering, please now provide us with your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The evacuation of the population to a different area could be described as humanitarian aid, but subject to certain conditions; that it happens in consultation with the population and all agencies and institutions. So I would not call this support, I would call it forced transport. And there was definitely no consultation with other parties, for them to be provided with support upon their arrival. So a unilateral effort at support is certainly not something that I would categorise as humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Boering. We will have a look at some footage tomorrow, and we will see everything in the movie that you saw, but my question in relation to everything that you've already seen during your preparation for testimony is whether General Nicolai and Colonel Karremans requested from the Army of Republika Srpska assistance in the transport of civilians from Potocari to the Federation, or, actually, to Kladanj, or not.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: That's perfectly possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Boering, in view of the fact that you were there, I must ask you whether this is possible or whether this is definitely so, since you were there, because later we are going to read to you the transcript of the conversation between General Mladic and Karremans. Can we look at P1008, please, in the e-court, so that the witness could see it. I'm not looking for any surprises. Thank you. This is page 19 in the English and page 16 in the Serbian, of this transcript. This is the transcript of the video footage that we are going to view tomorrow. I'm going to quote to you what General Mladic says: "What do you want?" He puts this question to Karremans. "You asked to meet. Let me hear what you want." And then Colonel Karremans says: "I had a talk with General Nicolai two hours ago and also with the national authorities about the request on behalf of the population. It's a request, and I'm not in a position to ask for anything."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We no longer have the original on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is a transcript of what you're going to look at tomorrow, because you said in your statement that this whole meeting was recorded. On the basis of what General Mladic said and what Colonel Karremans said, is it true - that's my question - that Colonel Karremans asked General Mladic for assistance pursuant to a request by General Nicolai? Because he said he had spoken also with the national authorities about the request on behalf of the population. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: There was some consultation between Nicolai and Karremans in the course of preparing for the meeting with Mladic, how the resources would be deployed, and that it was clear that the situation was hopeless, and DutchBat felt responsible, it was clear that DutchBat felt responsible for caring for all refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to read to you what Karremans says: "We, the command in Sarajevo, have said that the enclave has been lost and that I've been ordered by the B and H command of UNPROFOR to take care of all the refugees, and we are now approximately 10.000 women and children within the compound of Potocari, and the request of the B and H command, the command for Bosnia, is to negotiate about the conditions for the withdrawal of those people. There are some women who are able to speak English and what I've heard from all the soldiers --" could you please pay attention now -- "who are now working to, let's say, ease the pain for the population, is that they are waiting for buses to leave the enclave." So on the basis of this, my question is: Is Mr. Karremans informing General Mladic here about the kind of assistance they are asking for or that is needed and what the population needs? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Karremans is asking Mladic for support.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you were the civilian affairs person and in charge of contacts with the population, can you please tell us, how did Karremans find out what the population was requesting? Who prepared this information? Did he go and talk to the population or is this something that he received from the commander service that works with the population?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: In any case, during the preparations for this meeting, spokesmen had been selected from among the population, and they were consulted. There were three. Whether they had a full mandate and knew what it was all about, all three of them questioned that, but in any case, this was the best solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So was Colonel Karremans presenting his own position to General Mladic when he said to him, "Well, you wanted to meet, let's hear." That is the only thing that Mladic said and the rest was said by Karremans, so did he make his request on the basis of his own opinion or did he do that on the basis of the needs of the population and conversations with the civilian representatives? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I think the latter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If it's this other thing, that he said that on the basis of his conversation with the civilian population, did they then take part in the negotiations, in the conversations, and did he state their requests on the basis of what they said were the needs of the civilian population? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: In any case, they were also involved in the conversations with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Before meeting General Mladic, did they see Karremans? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: There was a preliminary meeting in the evening, before the one the next day at 10.00 a.m., but that preliminary meeting wasn't very long; there wasn't a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In one of our next sessions we are going to speak about these meetings. I am only now asking you about the resolution of the humanitarian catastrophe in which the population and the UNPROFOR found themselves. On page -- on a page of your 65 ter statement 06703, page 5, paragraph 6, you talk about this first -- alleged first meeting. Thank you. I'm going to remind you, during the examination-in-chief, Mr. Thayer asked you, on page 16 of the transcript, line 5, the following: "When you came for the negotiations at the Fontana, you saw the peacekeepers who were hostages." And then in line 13, on page 16, you gave a broader answer about how you spoke with that soldier and you said that you saw them all in one room. Do you remember that? Thank you. Can we show page 6 in the English, in the e-court, please. 5 in Serbian, 6 in the English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 16, line 13, you said there was a group of ten Dutch soldiers, they were sitting at a table, they were supposed to get food. They said that they were at the observation posts and that they were brought to Bratunac unwillingly. This is a quote from your testimony of today. Then it goes on to say, Well, we were not able to move freely, but we are going to quote that later. All right, I'm going to put a question to you now. I'm quoting now a part of your statement that you gave previously, on the 28th of September, 1995. You say, on page 5 - we have it in front of us - paragraph 6. This is this large last-but-one paragraph, actually, line 2, where you say: "I saw our fellow DutchBat soldiers, the hostages, sitting in a separate room in the hotel and briefly stopped to speak to them." Thank you. I have finished my quote. My question is: Were they in separate rooms?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
