utterances.text: In English, it's the third paragraph on that page and not the last-but-one, just to give the witness the opportunity to read it. Now continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you read this, Witness, sir? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Well, to be honest, it's rather obscure and fast. In any case, I've read one section, which is page 5; and the second part, I can't find that. I see only one section of text and I didn't see the second one. Or am I confused here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is the third paragraph on the screen in English. It begins with the words, "In Hotel Fontana we were received by Mladic." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the third section begins with "I saw our fellow DutchBat soldiers, the hostages, sitting in a separate room." That is -- you touched the screen and this is the result of that; it disappeared. It will come back very soon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No problem. That happens to nearly every witness. There we are again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the question of Mr. Tolimir was: Were they in separate rooms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think they were all in a single room.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that there were ten of them. Now, the hotel and the hotel room where you saw them, did it have ten beds? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: No. It was on the ground floor. In Hotel Fontana, there were rooms where groups could eat, a separate room for small receptions or small groups could do things. It was the ground floor. It wasn't intended for sleeping but for festivities, and I think that this room was one where ordinarily small groups could sit and eat too. I wasn't in a certain type of room that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in a room where they were seated at the table together.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you see them in a restaurant or in the rooms, the guest rooms, the bedrooms? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Hotel Fontana ground floor, an ordinary area where there are tables and chairs and people can eat there. There were definitely not any beds. That's how I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this portion of your statement, then, incorrect? Because there you say: "I saw our fellow DutchBat soldiers, the hostages, sitting in separate rooms in the hotel and I briefly stopped to speak to them."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, perhaps it's a translation issue. In the English text, it reads: "I saw our fellow DutchBat soldiers, the hostages, sitting in a separate room in the hotel." It is singular. Perhaps in the B/C/S, it's different, but the original English version speaks only about a room. That means one room.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We were provided the translation by the OTP, and the interpreters can see it and perhaps they can assist us. They can also see it on the screens and they can tell us how the second and third sentence of the third paragraph in English read, and in B/C/S does the second and third line in the penultimate paragraph. I can't speak any English so I'm just reading from what I was provided. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: In the B/C/S version, indeed, it says, "In separate rooms ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We received an explanation that in the B/C/S version it is a plural, it means several rooms. But the English version is the original version signed by the witness, and therefore, we should rely on that. And Mr. Boering provided us with this -- his knowledge on the top of his head. Please continue, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And thank you, Mr. Boering. Are you aware at all whether these soldiers actually got any sleep in those three days? Because you didn't see them in their bedrooms. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I didn't speak to them at length, but of course I asked how they were doing and they indicated that, as far as food and drink was concerned, they were being taken care of and that they could sleep but that they were definitely not -- they had no freedom of movement and they felt threatened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Boering. Would you now please take a look at the paragraph above the one we quoted from. It's a brief paragraph of three lines only. The first word reads, "For." And in B/C/S it's in four lines and it reads as follows: "At one point, we received a request from the hostages, members of the DutchBat, to meet with General Mladic in Bratunac. He himself was the one who was seeking to have this meeting. Sometime in the evening I drove to Bratunac together with Karremans and Sergeant Major Raven [sic]." Now, my question to you is: Was this, as far as you can recall, the first meeting that you had with General Mladic or not?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. A few moments ago, we saw the transcript where it said I said that General Mladic said, "What is it that you want? You were asking for a meeting." Now, would General Mladic have put that question or those questions if he was the one who actually initiated this meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: That doesn't sound logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it possible, do you allow for the possibility, that you actually mistook this activity and this meeting for something else, because all of the witnesses who appeared to testify here only spoke about three meetings between Karremans and General Mladic in Fontana, and we've had a number of witnesses here who testified to that. Is it possible that you may have made a mistake because, from what you're saying, it would appear that there were four meetings held and not three.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: No. There were three meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you say that there were three meetings. Would you please read through your statement for tomorrow and then, as you read through it, perhaps you can draw a conclusion as to the number of meetings. There was a meeting, this one in the evening, then at 10.00, and then there was a meeting with interpreters, and then there was another one on the next day. So that would mean four meetings. "Yes" or "no." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I suggest that instead of giving the witness homework to do tonight, that if General Tolimir is seriously suggesting that somehow this witness statement or the witness has claimed at any time that there were four meetings at the Hotel Fontana rather than three, that he take the time to do it now. And if that is indeed the position of the Defence, that they believe that this witness at any time has said that there were four meetings at the Hotel Fontana, then he should just put that to the witness and deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir started to do that already, but to avoid any more discussion about that, Mr. Boering, can you tell me again, there were three Hotel Fontana meetings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How many of them did you attend personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. And I thank Mr. Thayer. My apologies to the witness. My intentions were good. I didn't have any bad intentions, because I really read through his statement carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But now if we look at page 6, we see that the witness says in the first sentence, and I'm reading from the Serbian -- could we please have page 6 in the Serbian?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We need both versions on the screen first.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English, it's the same page, and it starts with the word -- the paragraph starting with the words, "A film crew ..." Thank you, Mr. President. In Serbian, that's the first paragraph on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It reads as follows: "A film crew recorded the entire discussion." My question is this: I don't want to have arguments here, and I am in no way disputing or doubting what you're saying, but perhaps tomorrow we can see a video clip and then perhaps this will help you refresh your memory and maybe then we will get out of this situation easily. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, what is the question for the witness? We see the paragraph you are referring to on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What is your question to the witness? The witness is now available for answering any questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was the first meeting filmed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I have to think long and hard. Just a moment. I saw film crews on multiple occasions. At the specific moment, it's not rock solid in my memory, but I seem to remember that the first time I entered, that Mladic, Karremans, Rave were certainly present and I believe there was a film crew there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for your answer, Mr. Boering. Would you now please take a look on the same page that you have before you, and in Serbian that's the second paragraph, on the page that I have before me, so would you look at the following paragraph. There it says the following: "During the discussion, a pig was slaughtered outside." Can you remember whether this pig was slaughtered on the occasion when you had -- during the time when you had that first meeting with Mladic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I think this was at one of the later meetings, but -- and I think that a representative of the Muslims was present there as well and he wasn't present at the first meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you allow for the possibility that you may be referring to something else here, because there were no Muslims present, where you talk about the slaughtering of the pig? Because if we look at the next paragraph -- could we have the next page in English, please, and leave the same page in Serbian. In other words, could we have page 7 in English and 6 should remain in Serbian because it is already on the screen. Thank you. Here, we see, in the next paragraph -- thank you -- well, I don't have the -- I don't have -- my screen is dead. Thank you. While we wait for the image to come up -- and I don't have the image on my screen, it's black completely. Thank you. Now, you say: "When we returned to the compound, back at the compound, I chose a man to act as spokesman for the Muslims. I chose this particular man because I knew that he had been the headmaster of the school in Srebrenica. I had occasionally chatted with him and had the idea that he would be a suitable person to negotiate with Mladic." My question: Did you choose a person who would negotiate -- who would participate in the negotiations after the first meeting with Mladic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And during that first meeting, did you hear that pig being slaughtered that I mentioned in the earlier paragraph, where you said, "During our conversation, somebody slaughtered a pig outside"? So could the Muslims actually hear this slaughtering of the pig?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: As I said earlier, I thought that was at the second meeting, but at this point it's not rock solid in my memory and I'll have to read my statement. I haven't done that yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I proposed that, however, Mr. Thayer did not agree with that. Now, can we see the next paragraph, the one following the one that I just quoted: "At about 2300 hours I again departed for Bratunac together with Karremans. At a Serbian check-point I was told that I should bring a spokesman with me. I then drove back and fetched the spokesman." Did you set out for this second meeting at 2300 hours without a spokesman? And what is it, in fact, that you understand as "spokesman"?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: At the second meeting which we are referring to, the spokesman is the person involved who ultimately came along. That's the teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I quoted from a paragraph a little earlier where you mentioned that headmaster, but now let me ask you this: Do you know how this man was found in Potocari, when you say that you chose this man to be the spokesman? Were you the one who actually went out looking for such person or was it someone else?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Together with Sergeant Major Rave, I consulted who would be the best spokesman, and in accommodating the Muslim population near the compound, we noticed him and knew roughly where we could find him, and if I remember correctly, I asked Sergeant Major Rave to go get him and bring him to me so that we could prepare. I don't remember whether I accompanied him, whether we did that together, but that doesn't really matter so much to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I agree with you, it's probably not important, but tell me, did Mr. Mandzic actually oppose being the representative who would talk with Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not hear the last portion of the question. Could it be repeated, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could you please repeat the last portion of your question; the interpreter didn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will repeat my whole question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did Nesib Mandzic actually oppose being the representative who would talk with Mladic? Because you told us a moment ago that you and Mr. Rave actually briefed him or prepared him for the meeting.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I remember that we asked him and that after some deliberation he consented, but it did bother him. And that's why he asked for some more latitude later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you referring that he needed some more time to think it over or that he needed some space in order to consult with someone else? So what do you mean exactly by "latitude?"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or "space" in Serbian, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He wanted to have more people present in the consultation so that he would not be the only one to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we need the second break now. Sir, we must have the second break. We will resume at quarter past 6.00 for the final session of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could I ask e-court to return this page 6 that we had in the Serbian, that we were looking at before the break, and that is page 8 in the English, so that the witness can see what we are going to be discussing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, this is 65 ter 6703.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I forgot to say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We always can cooperate in these situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Boering, please, when we look at this statement of yours, there is a certain rearrangement of activities from one section to another, or from one part to another, and there are some things that are illogical and you said that yourself. It's not logical for Mladic to say, "All right, what would you -- what do you want?" And then for you to say, "What do you want?" So I'm asking you this: All the meetings that you and Karremans and Mr. Rave had with General Mladic, were all of those meetings recorded with a camera?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: At this time, I don't know that. Often they were, but whether they always were, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I'm not sure if you have the right page in English on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'm just going to look at that now. We are looking at the place where it says, "Around 2300 hours." This is the third paragraph in English. So this is the paragraph that I wanted the witness to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, since you say you are not sure, can you please tell us whether, on the 10th or between the 11th and the 12th, did you have two or three meetings with Mladic? And would this help you to remember?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I had three meetings, at least meetings where I was present, with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was anyone else present with you, of the UNPROFOR representatives, at these three meetings? Could you tell us who else was with you from UNPROFOR at the meetings?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: If you're referring to UNPROFOR DutchBat, Karremans was present at all meetings. And Sergeant Major Rave was present certainly at two of the three meetings. The third, I'd have to read up on that. It's possible that he was present at all three. I almost think he was. And if you are referring to UNPROFOR, you could say that the interpreter Petar, who was paid by UNPROFOR, was present as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you remember who was with you at the first meeting with General Mladic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes. At the first meeting, I was with Rave and Karremans, and Mladic had some people with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this meeting recorded with a camera? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the witness has answered this question before the break. He was not sure about that and then he tried to think about that, and he provided us with an answer already.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Since the witness already answered, I'm just going back to say that on page 6 he said that a film crew or a TV crew recorded the whole conversation. This is why I'm asking, because then it seems that there were four meetings. With the best of intentions, I would like to clarify the situation so that we could discuss this. It's not my aim to compromise or discredit the witness. Anyone can fail to remember the chronological sequence of things. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At the moment, we have a problem with the transcript. I don't see Mr. Tolimir speaking in e-court -- in LiveNote, sorry. Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, I would like to know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have the transcript in LiveNote still working but it's stopped in e-court. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to know, other than General Tolimir's saying so, or perhaps his confusion, what his basis is for again suggesting that there were four meetings, or that this witness somehow has ever said that there were any more than three meetings. Trial transcript is before the Trial Chamber. General Tolimir knows that this witness has testified in two prior trials and has given uncountable statements, all of which he said there are three meetings. That has never been in doubt. The witness has stated on a number of occasions today that there were three meetings. So unless we get right down to whatever is behind General Tolimir's insinuation that there are four meetings, we are wasting time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, can you tell us what is the background of your questioning in this respect? The witness indeed - I agree with Mr. Thayer - stated several times that he took part in three Hotel Fontana meetings, and as far as he is able to recall, they were all filmed by a crew. Only in respect of the first meeting he was not quite sure if that is really the case. What is the problem or the background or the purpose of your questioning?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The purpose of my questions is that the witness said that in the evening on the 11th, he was with General Mladic at the Hotel Fontana. Then he said that Rave, Karremans, the witness, and Mr. -- and the spokesperson were there. Then he said again that they were there on the 10th. This is the third meeting. And then he said he didn't remember whether a meeting was recorded or not. If he doesn't remember it being recorded, and says that the observers scheduled that meeting, I wanted to clear up whether it was the first meeting when General Mladic asked Karremans what it was all about. If we don't clarify this, then you will see that there will be a problem later. I can leave it like this and you can judge the weight. I'm not -- it is not my intention to compromise the witness. I can help him. If Mr. Thayer thinks that we can resolve this matter by aggravating the situation, I can move on to something else and then later you can make your own judgement on this matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't see Mr. Thayer to aggravate the situation. Nobody is in that position. We just want to clarify the situation. May I, to avoid further discussions on that, just ask the

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: the Hotel Fontana and that you attended all three meetings? I already asked you that. And if you recall that there were -- was always a team of people filming the meetings. Could you clarify that a last time, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember that there were three meetings. I remember, as you indicated, seeing the film crew several times. Whether they were present at all three, I assume they were. Certainly at the first, and also later, they were present. Certainly at the third meeting, because I remember that a Srebrenica sign and a register of marriages was presented to the lady present, to show, "I know when you were married," and that's been established on record. As for the second time, whether there was a film crew present, that was that evening at 11 p.m., it's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you certain that the second meeting was in the evening at 11.00?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. 10.00, 11.00. In the evening, yes. And the third meeting was the next day at 10.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on. Before you do that, let me put a last question to the witness: Can you tell me, have you ever heard about a fourth meeting in the Hotel Fontana, between UNPROFOR representatives and General Mladic and his officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the third meeting, I left the enclave fairly quickly and, of course, there were meetings afterwards in Fontana later on, with other UNPROFOR people as well. So of course there were meetings after that too. That might explain the misunderstanding. General Nicolai and others were present there as well, but I was not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have again a problem with the transcript, but we can follow in LiveNote. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm now asking the witness: On the basis of all that has been said, are you sure that Mladic asked you to come to the meeting or was it what we saw earlier when Mr. Mladic -- or General Mladic said, "What is it? You wanted to see me." So what was it? Was it the way you described it on page 6, paragraph 5, of the Serbian version, and on page 6 of the English version, paragraph 3?

utterances.speaker: Do you stand by that, that there have been three meetings in
utterances.text: I remember that this issue came up at previous testimony as well, and at the time I indicated that I was not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you are not certain, would you be certain if you were to look at all three footage -- all the footage of all the three meetings, from the beginning to the end? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this is really speculation. How can the witness say, "I will be certain if I see that and that"? You should wait with this question, after putting this to the witness, by showing a video.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. There is no need to defend the witness from me. We are going to show that tomorrow. We will not be going into that today. We are going to move to a new group of questions and then the witness could reply to this matter tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I can't accept this statement. I'm not defending a witness. This is really not correct to put that on the record. Nobody will be defended except you. You are the accused and you may defend yourself, with the assistance of your team. The question was different. The question -- your question was not appropriate to say, "Will you be certain after having seen something"? This is speculation. This is not an appropriate question to the witness at this point in time. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'm not going to be speculating anymore. Since I'm the only problem here and no one else, I'm go be leaving this for tomorrow after we watch the footage. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My next question for you is this: According to your information, who organised the meetings between General Mladic and Colonel Karremans? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Do you stand by that, that there have been three meetings in
utterances.text: Well, the second and third meetings were clearly organised at General Mladic's request. The first, as I've explained earlier, is unclear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you able to tell us who invited the people and escorted them to the meeting? The first meeting is what I'm thinking of, since you're not sure.

utterances.speaker: Do you stand by that, that there have been three meetings in
utterances.text: Conceivably the first meeting was arranged by Petar or our own DutchBat soldiers that had been taken hostage, and as for being escorted to the first meeting, we drove ourselves in two cars. We had no escort. We drove ourselves. And en route to that meeting we were stopped at some points and we explained where we were headed and they let us pass after some consultation. We certainly were not escorted on the way there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, since your testimony is very important about whose initiative the meeting was, because many things depend on this, it's very important for us to know certain things, so it's not a good idea to say that I'm not sure about something or not so, but you -- that's why I'm putting these questions to which you gave the answers that you gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, no testimony of a witness would be helpful for your purpose or anybody's purpose if the witness would tell you something which seems to be certain if the witness is not in a position to say that. If he says, "I'm not sure about that," you must take it like that. The witness is sitting here and is trying to, in most cases, trying to help you with what he has in mind and what he recalls. Please don't judge in that way about the answer you have got from the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I am not judging anything. I was just saying that, in view of his answers, that I'm not going to put any more questions about that. I would like the e-court now to show page 3 of this statement that we are looking at in the Serbian, paragraph 1, and it's probably page 3 in the English, but it's a different paragraph. When I look at the text, I will be able to tell where it is. Thank you. We can now see it on our screens in both versions. On page 2 in the Serbian translation, you started saying something about a person called Sarkic and then you go on to say that: "He seemed to be friendly, but I heard that he was an unreliable person who was trigger-happy or hungry for combat. I heard that from my predecessor. I had very little occasion to meet with him. I only spoke with him in January and June [as interpreted]. The area where he was deployed was not easily accessible and it was constantly in wartime conditions. There were Muslim fighters there and Serbs and Muslims exchanged fire all the time."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not have the original on the screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is on the screen as the second paragraph which begins with, "Sarkic" and it was quite fine, the interpretation, without one word. "I only spoke to him in January and July," I can read on the screen it was interpreted or quoted by Mr. Tolimir, I don't know that, as June instead of July. Just for the record. Mr. Tolimir, continue, please, or put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us why it was, what was the reason, that you had such infrequent contacts with Mr. Sarkic? Was it because of his personality or was it because he was in an unaccessible area? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Do you stand by that, that there have been three meetings in
utterances.text: We had no contact with the Milici Brigade at all, and this was in part because we had insufficient access to that area, because there were borders within the enclave known as the Bandera Triangle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was he within the so-called Bandera Triangle or outside of it on the other side of the separation line, the side where the Serbian army was deployed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Do you stand by that, that there have been three meetings in
utterances.text: Yes. He was on the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, since you mention Bandera Triangle, tell us why it was that you couldn't go through or you couldn't cross over Bandera Triangle and go about your business. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Do you stand by that, that there have been three meetings in
utterances.text: We were more limited in our operations there. We had some observation posts but we did not have true freedom of movement there. This was because of the Muslim leader, Zulfo, who was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain to this Trial Chamber why Zulfo had prohibited you from moving in the area of responsibility of his brigade and within the so-called Bandera Triangle?

utterances.speaker: Do you stand by that, that there have been three meetings in
utterances.text: He wanted to handle things independently, and tolerated no supervision or control, and he didn't want this from Naser Oric or, later on, from anybody else in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of what you've just said, can you tell us whether you had informed the UNPROFOR command and the Main Staff that you did not have access to the area of responsibility -- to the area of responsibility of the brigade, the 281st Brigade? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Do you stand by that, that there have been three meetings in
utterances.text: Well, first, it was not my job to report that. That was up to my commander, Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans, and he most certainly did report that. And subsequently, we tried to patrol more extensively in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Under the agreement, it was your task to monitor the demilitarisation of the area of responsibility -- of the zone. Did that imply that you should have the freedom of movement throughout the entire safe area?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The accused used the word "zone."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's what it meant, and that's why the decision was taken to patrol more in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what happened once you set off on your patrols?

utterances.speaker: Do you stand by that, that there have been three meetings in
utterances.text: Yes. At a certain point one of those patrols was stopped and prevented from proceeding. We weren't allowed to go any further. And there was no opportunity to return either, so it was a type of hostage situation. Concerning the group that was patrolling there, that is. And then I drove there in a vehicle to try to solve the problem, and in the end, after a few days, we were free to continue our duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness. I have a very small question. In the document that we have on the screen, on page 3, regarding Zulfo, you say that you had no contact with him and that he worked in a region or zone called the Bandera Triangle. Where does this name come from? Do you know why it's called the Bandera Triangle? Who came up with the word in the first place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I think it was the region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So far, no witness has been able to tell us where the name came from. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In lines 1 through 5, on page 67 of today's transcript, just a moment ago, you said that later on you tried to conduct the patrols. Can you tell us whether you were able to conduct patrols in the Bandera Triangle and did you have access to it at all or was it a no-pass zone?

utterances.speaker: Do you stand by that, that there have been three meetings in
utterances.text: In the efforts to gain extensive access, this patrol that we just mentioned was en route, and was blocked. So there were means to use certain roads but not all areas were accessible, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you say that you didn't have access to all areas, could you tell us which places you had no access to and where you could not send your patrols? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Do you stand by that, that there have been three meetings in
utterances.text: In the border region, there were some observation posts where we could go, we could get to them by roads that we were allowed to move on. And as for knowing for certain how far you could deviate from those paths, I don't have that information, but it was a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether, in the Bandera Triangle, it was you who were being checked or did you actually carry out checks on Zulfo's men in Bandera Triangle?

utterances.speaker: Do you stand by that, that there have been three meetings in
utterances.text: You could say, on the border of the enclave, from the observation posts, we could do our work. There were areas where we were not in a position to perform true inspections.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether you know why you were not allowed to go into certain areas, as you've just told us a moment ago? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Do you stand by that, that there have been three meetings in
utterances.text: It may have related to smuggling efforts or possible breakouts from the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say that this had to do with smuggling, do you mean that there was drug smuggling? Was there smuggling of people or weapons? What was it that you actually monitored? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Do you stand by that, that there have been three meetings in
utterances.text: Definitely smuggling of arms. That was certainly monitored. Smuggling of goods? Well, I haven't seen a lot of reports on the actions against that but, of course, due to lack of resources, there were smuggling routes to bring goods inside, supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If there was weapons trafficking there, do you know what measures UNPROFOR took in order to enable the monitoring of the area where possible arms were being trafficked? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Do you stand by that, that there have been three meetings in
utterances.text: Well, that's what we used the observation posts and patrols for.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, did the UNPROFOR command in Tuzla, Sarajevo and Zagreb know, were they informed, that you did not have access to all areas within the demilitarised zone in Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Do you stand by that, that there have been three meetings in
utterances.text: I think that they were definitely informed about the hostage-taking that occurred in the Bandera Triangle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether the Security Council, the UN Security Council, was aware of the problem?

utterances.speaker: Do you stand by that, that there have been three meetings in
utterances.text: No. I have no idea about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether your command proposed that the matter be resolved at joint meetings between the warring parties that were being held in Sarajevo? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Do you stand by that, that there have been three meetings in
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know why the VRS was never aware of that and yet it was one of the parties' signatories of that, just as was the Muslim side and the UNPROFOR? And I'm referring here to the agreement on demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: Do you stand by that, that there have been three meetings in
utterances.text: What I remember is that I most certainly did speak with Major Nikolic about it, that we had been detained in the Bandera Triangle, so the VRS knew about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you speak with Nikolic, and did you tell him that you had absolutely no access to certain areas within the triangle and that there was some weapons trafficking going on there? Thank you.
